audio_caption: The audio clip starts with a male speaker expressing fascination with "Tolkiin himself," recalling the privilege of attending lectures on English at Oxford. He then mentions Dennis Gerolt, who spoke to Tolkiin about his writing and work, specifically how the "epic mythology was created in the mind of a professor of English language." The speaker maintains a respectful and slightly reverent tone throughout this description.

The audio clip begins with a male speaker discussing "The Hobbit" and its well-made mythology. He mentions having a "scheme" to work from and admits that he "got sucked into it," much like the hobbit himself got moving out into the world. He notes that his characters and story "took charge," elaborating that he was not completely under their spell, dismissing that he was dreaming at all or undergoing an "obsession." Instead, he describes it as a "sensation" when developing his ideas, comparing the writing process to figuring out whether "A, B, C, D, or E, one of them is right." The clip concludes with an audio cue, resembling a low-frequency "beep."

The audio clip predominantly features a single male speaker with a measured and contemplative tone. He explains that he used maps to develop a complex story and reflects on the chronology of his work, specifically mentioning the year 1942 and discussing revisions to the work. The speaker also recounts how he typed his work out twice and made mistakes. He mentions that he used "stood as a past passive." The audio includes intermittent laughter and chuckle sounds, suggesting moments of humor or lightheartedness. The speech is clear and audible, but background sounds are minimal, creating an intimate, reflective atmosphere.

The audio clip begins with two speakers, a male interviewer and author J.R.R. Tolkien, engaged in a conversation. The interviewer questions, "Do you feel any sense of guilt at all…you've devoted a large part of your life to a fictional thing?" Tolkien chuckles and retorts, "No, I quite...there's quite a lot of linguistic wisdom in it." He then expresses that he doesn't feel guilt. The interviewer follows up on fondness for homely things of life, for "pipe and fire and bed," and Tolkien agrees, saying, "You have a particular fondness...that's why I feel at home." He explains that the Shire from his stories is like a world he first became aware of. He adds that it's very like the world he was born into, but perhaps more poignant because he wasn't born there and that he was born in South Africa, even though he returned to England when he was very young. He concludes that the Shire's influence bit into his memory and imagination.

The audio begins with a male speaker discussing "first Christmas trees, wilting eucalyptus," and how heat and sand can suddenly lead to a "Worcestershire village". He touches upon a love for "central Midland English" countryside with good water stones, elder trees, and small rivers. The speaker then asks, "at what age did you come to England?" The same male voice responds stating he was three-and-a-half when he first left. The speaker goes on to talk about memory, comparing it to a photograph where constantly taking pictures in the same place can blur the image. He shares a vivid memory of a house from childhood, but now understands it to be a "best-ish" combination of his own home and his grandmother's. The speaker affirms that he remembers things "extremely well", citing bathing in the Indian Ocean when he was nearly two, as a very clear memory.

The audio clip features a conversation between two speakers, one male, one of unknown gender, the second speaking in a slightly more formal and academic tone. The conversation begins with a question to the other speaker about the burden of the ring, focusing on "long suffering," "perseverance," "merit," and the character being "almost a Christ figure." The speaker responds, stating that they "didn't do much choosing," having simply continued from where the Hobbit left off. There is an admission that the speaker has gotten the "Hobbits on my hand." The first speaker agrees, but emphasizes that, despite the "appalling danger," the character struggles on and continues, which the second speaker describes as more like "allegory of the human race." The recording ends with an expression of being impressed by the character.

The audio clip begins with a male speaker discussing how people survive against impossible odds. He speaks with a thoughtful tone. He continues by pondering if Midgard might be Middle Earth, and answers by describing that they are in fact the same word, and that people mistakenly assume Middle Earth is another planet. The speaker says it's simply an old-fashioned word for "this world we live in," emphasizing that it is imagined as surrounded by the ocean.

The audio clip begins with a male speaker reflecting on Middle-earth and its connection to our world, stating that it seemed to be "this world we live in" but at a "different era". He proceeds to inquire about the intentions behind specific races embodying certain principles, such as "elves, wisdom; the dwarfs, craftsmanship," and men representing "husbandry and battle". The speaker maintains a neutral and inquisitive tone. Following this, we hear another male speaker presumably about to respond.

The clip features a single male speaker with a thoughtful and articulate tone discussing the creation of different races, emphasizing the need to make them distinct and the desire to have greater power of mind. He mentions immortality and longevity in relation to elves, describing them as very longeval, and contrasts them with dwarves, whom he likens to the Jewish people. The speaker reflects on the Semitic origins of both the Jews and the Dwarves.

The clip begins with a male speaker theorizing about why resting English people are made small in size in some artistic depictions, suggesting it reflects the "small reach of their imagination." He clarifies that this does not reflect the "small reach of their courage or latent power." The speaker emphasizes that this observation constitutes one of the great strengths of a particular book, despite its "enormous conglomeration of names." Another male speaker then says "finally" .

The audio clip features a conversation between two speakers, a man and a woman. The man, who speaks with a calm and articulate tone, expresses that starting with a name helps him produce a story. The woman then asks the man about which languages helped him when writing the Lord of the Rings. The man mentions that Welsh was always attractive, and states "the music of Welsh comes through in the names".

The clip begins with a male speaker acknowledging something. He then indicates he is aware, but it's "very potent". The same male speaker then is asked if a book is to be considered as an allegory and he replies "no".

The audio begins with a male speaker, who mentions something that smells like "eucalyptus," suggesting an indoor or garden environment. The speaker is then interviewed by another male speaker, regarding themes in his book, the decline of the third age, and the possibility of a fourth age. The interviewer cites Tennyson and asks if God exists in "The Lord of the Rings." The speaker responds saying "He is mentioned once or twice" and describes himself as "a Roman Catholic." The first male speaker then poses a hypothetical question: "I should be remembered chiefly by writings on philology or The Lord of the Rings and the Hobbit?" To this question, the interviewee remarks that people "would probably forget he was professor of modern languages."
